title: Starting out
author: Specialist-Theory351
selftext:
Hello,

Me and my friend just started building a rpg game like Diablo 2 entirely with ai, there are already a few roadblocks that we have hit. We have no coding or game development experience.

We are using grok/cursor and slack with the goddot engine.

What is the best way to generate visuals? Our game plan was to build one village that will be our starting village, one character, and some enemies outside the village to kill. We used meshy/grok to build tiles to use to build the village and it seems super bulky, time consuming and the end result leaves alot to be desired.

The first character we built looks cool and the first enemy but we dont know how to make the fighting feel more natural, the animations of the fighting are super clunky and the enemy moonwalks to us backwards. Any advice here?

It also uses up our cursor credits really fast is there a better way to stack this that is more efficient? Im sure we have started everything wrong but were having fun, we just need a bit of direction.

comments.author: Gigaslavx
comments.body: Hi sounds like there's close to no progress atm not sure you will learn much here from short responses, you're better off watching guides even just on youtube is good enough as visual reference as well as asking the ai itself

replies.author: Specialist-Theory351
replies.body: Yes my main concern is that we are completely off track and what were doing is completely inefficient, we've only been going a few days so I was hoping if there was a much better stack or way of building a 3d isometric Diablo like that we could not have to completely scrap the project and start again in a few months

replies.author: Gigaslavx
replies.body:
Start with the foundation, don't rush

If you want to make a disposable messy prototype to see if the main game idea is even fun to begin with before building the whole game that's also a big plus especially if you're just starting out even a web concept

Not sure how much expertise in game dev or even programming you have but if close to 0 and most of is not ai assisted but made well... it's going to be a long and painful and expensive path very easy to steer of course and end up in a literal ditch where it's impossible to get out from

Start with the foundation of the game the boring technical stuff before all the fun things even begin depends on the game be it pooling/decoupling/batching/culling etc

If you start doing things in wrong orders of layers as well as cutting corners you will have very shaky incompatible foundation where things will work in a moment but the second you start making any changes everything will start crumbling down

comments.author: boatwash
comments.body: Honestly I’d recommend just learning the basics of blender. It’ll take a while but also it’s a free program! And LLMs can help teach you how to use it

replies.author: boatwash
replies.body: You can use something like meshy or another AI tool to build models, then rig and animate them in blender. I’d just put like 1-2 hours a day into it for a week and see what happens

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
I’ll give you some advice from an experienced game producer. I’ve been doing this all my life and it’s still hard. But you need to identify the core game loop. That is not a cliché, this is an important goal for you. You have to define what it is that will drive the player to continue playing. Are they chasing items? Are they chasing level ups? Are they unlocking new abilities you cannot count on the player to just want to kill enemies and go sightseeing in your game. If you can identify that overarching system that compels the player to keep playing then this will help you focus on what’s most important. 

More specifically to this type of game, that main gameplay hook needs to feel good attacking enemies defeating them getting power ups and items needs to feel really rewarding and it needs to feel challenging so I would suggest that you build one or two types of enemies maybe a close range enemy and a arranged enemy set up a few encounters and allow the player to fight for their life. Once that feels good then add more variables like hazards new enemy types, puzzles, locked door, incremental objectives, like turning off hazards, finding key objects to unlock areas.

For art design, we like to use this term of setting a visual target, some designers would say to create a beautiful corner in the painting focus on what the final outcome should look like, and this will help you set the standard for your art production however you attempt to achieve this with AI. You should have screenshots of games for reference. Go on Midjourney or ChatGPT and create concept art for characters locations key items. 

For story and progression, you should identify important beats that you would like the character to go through if there was a battle or a moral choice or a confrontation that you imagine when you were creating this game concept flesh that out and use that to set the tone for the game.

For the UX and UI take a look at your favorite games or games that inspired you to create this game take screenshots of their interface, their inventory systems, their main menus their settings, their quest screens and take what you like. Identify the key features and feed that into your AI model.

For sound design, I think you can worry about that later, but I would not focus on AI to do your sound effects and music. I think this is just a human touch that you’ll want to look into later.

comments.author: Faratas14
comments.body:
The keyword Is Iteration.

You should look for reference, moodboard, basic instruction. Check Itch.io and look under bundles or UI items.

Use an Image Generator to get a "final result", else you can find yourself running circles.

And write. Keep your choices and ideas tracked, so you can iterate the same thing as long as you get what you want.

comments.body:

comments.author: Nilo_Team
comments.body:
hey- meshy tile grinding is real-

nilo.io is free in the browser (monthly bits)- gen the village props / character / enemies there, hit model settings + LOD to cut polys, export GLB/FBX into Godot. auto-rig is bipedal T-pose only so your hero + humanoid enemies land cleaner (no quadruped/creature rigs yet).

won't fix the moonwalk combat feel by itself (that's anim/controller in-engine) but the mesh gen → export loop stops being the bulky part. LMK :)
